Consonantal i

SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

love verb and noun

also be fond of, fondness

classical

Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
Ter. Ph. 478: omnēs vōs amō

amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum

verb, first conjugation

Of people and of things (rūs amat, Ov. Met. 14.627). In comedy and Cicero’s letters amō tē also thanks (Meritō tē amō, Ter. Ad. 945–946), and amābō is “please” (see please).

Examples

  • nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō

    For I won’t grant that you love him more than I do.Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7

  • Mī Geta, omnēs vōs amō.

    My dear Geta, I love you all.Ter. Ph. 478

  • dīlēxī tum tē nōn tantum ut vulgus amīcam, sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs

    I loved you then not just as the crowd loves a girlfriend, but as a father loves his sons and sons-in-law.Catull. 72.3–4

  • nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē: hoc tantum possum dīcere, nōn amō tē

    I don’t love you, Sabidius, and I can’t say why; all I can say is this: I don’t love you.Mart. 1.32.1–2

Other words

  • amor, amōris m. — love

    noun, third declension · classical · Cic. Off. 1.12: praecipuum quendam amōrem in eōs quī prōcreātī sunt

    Also of the one loved: dēliciīs atque amōribus meīs (Cic. Att. 16.6.4).

  • dīligō, dīligere, dīlēxī, dīlēctum — love, hold dear

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Catull. 72.4: sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs; Cic. Fam. 16.2.1: quantum mē dīligis; Traupman 98: to be fond of, dīligō

    Lewis & Short: “to value or esteem highly, to love”: the love of regard and choice, as of a father for his children in Catullus.

See also I love you, hate, kiss, hug, darling, please.
